notes.meaning: "The third day" means the third day of the fast Esther had asked the Jews to keep. She took off her mourning clothes and put on her royal robes. She wanted to win the favour of the man who was both her husband and her king. She went while her prayers were still fresh, and her time with God made her bold. The king's throne faced the entrance, so he would see her as she stood there, waiting between hope and fear.

The king was pleased to see her. The sources say it was God who turned his heart, since a king's heart is in the Lord's hand. Holding out the gold scepter meant that her coming uninvited was forgiven and that she was welcome. Touching its tip, and perhaps kissing it, was her way of showing thanks and respect.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic Bibles include a longer Greek telling of this scene. In it Esther faints at the king's angry look, and then God makes him gentle. He leaps up and holds her until she recovers. Protestant commentators such as Matthew Henry know this account but treat it as outside the Bible.

notes.meaning: "Up to half the kingdom" is a figure of speech. It means nothing reasonable would be refused. Esther had feared for her life, and now she was promised whatever she asked. God often calms his people's fears and goes beyond their hopes. Matthew Henry adds that Esther came to a proud king, but we come to a God of love. We also have an Advocate, someone who speaks for us, and that is Jesus.

Esther asked only that the king and Haman come to a meal. Honouring the king's favourite would please the king. It also kept Haman from growing suspicious. And it meant Haman would be there when she spoke, so she could accuse him to his face. She wanted the best moment to make her real request.
The king had Haman fetched quickly so Esther's wish could be carried out. He came at once. That showed he still felt kindly toward her. He would not have accepted her meal if he meant her harm.
The "banquet of wine" was the part of the meal after the food, when fruit and wine were served. In that cheerful moment the king asked again what Esther wanted. He repeated his generous promise.

Esther began, "This is my petition," and then stopped. She did not think the time was right. She simply asked them to come back the next day. The sources give several reasons. Perhaps she was nervous, or wanted more time to pray. Perhaps she wanted to win the king's heart further. Above all, God's quiet guiding (often called providence) was at work. The night in between would bring the events of chapter 6.

Haman left the meal delighted. But at the gate Mordecai would not stand or tremble before him. Mordecai acted from conscience. He was not afraid of Haman, and he trusted God to save his people. The higher Haman rose, the less he could stand being slighted, and he was filled with rage.

Haman held himself back. He could easily have struck Mordecai down, but he was waiting for the day set to destroy all the Jews. Wesley sees God's hand here, making Haman tie his own hands. At home he called his friends and his wife Zeresh to pour out his feelings and plan.

Haman boasted of his wealth, his many sons (ten, as chapter 9 shows), and his high rank. Persians counted many sons a great honour. The Geneva Notes warn that when wicked people are raised up, they often grow proud and cruel instead of humble.

Being the only guest with the king and queen was a great honour, and Haman was thrilled. He thought the queen was charmed by him. In truth she meant to accuse him. Her invitation was really a summons to judgment. He boasted about the very thing that would bring him down.

All Haman's riches and honours meant nothing to him while Mordecai sat at the gate. A small slight, which a humble man would barely notice, tormented this proud man. Proud people may have much of what they want, but if they don't have it all, it feels like nothing. Adam Clarke adds that the soul was made for God, and only God can truly fill it.

Zeresh and his friends told Haman to set up a pole about 75 feet high and ask the king the next morning to have Mordecai killed on it. They took it for granted that the king would agree. The great height was meant to shame Mordecai in front of everyone and to frighten Haman's enemies. The word "gallows" simply means wood or a pole, and some think impaling was meant. Haman went to bed pleased, never dreaming he would be the first to die on it.
